title: Disequilibrium calorimetry for determination of ultrasonic power in sonochemistry
author: Plattes, Köhler, et al.
materials: A glass beaker (100 ml) was filled with 40 ml deionized water with a temperature lower than the temperature of the ultrasonic bath (VWR Ultrasonic Cleaner USC-TH, 45 kHz, 180 W). The beaker was then placed in the ultrasonic bath and the bath was switched on. The temperature rise in the beaker and the bath was recorded using two thermocouple type thermometers that had a precision of 0.1 °C (VWR Traceable Monitoring Thermometer). The experiment was repeated 5 times. A typical result is shown as example in Fig. 1.Fig. 1Typical temperature rises in the beaker and the ultrasonic bath during disequilibrium calorimetry.Fig. 1

steps.title: Prepare water sample in beaker
steps.instruction: Fill a 100 ml glass beaker with 40 ml deionized water whose temperature is lower than the temperature of the ultrasonic bath.

steps.title: Set up ultrasonic bath and thermometers
steps.instruction: Place the beaker in the VWR Ultrasonic Cleaner USC‑TH (45 kHz, 180 W). Insert two VWR Traceable Monitoring Thermometers (thermocouple type, 0.1 °C precision) – one probe into the water in the beaker and the other into the bath – to record temperature continuously.

steps.title: Run calorimetry measurement
steps.instruction: Switch on the ultrasonic bath and sonicate, recording the temperature rise of both the beaker and the bath until thermal equilibrium is approached. Perform the complete measurement five times.

steps.title: Determine temperature intercept and slope
steps.instruction: Observe that the beaker temperature curve follows a second‑order polynomial while the bath temperature rises linearly. Note that the two temperatures intersect at 20 °C after 250 s of sonication (longer if the initial beaker temperature is below 12 °C). Interpolate the slope (dT1/dt) of the beaker temperature at this intercept.

steps.title: Calculate ultrasonic power
steps.instruction: Calculate power using P = cP × m × (dT1/dt), where cP = 4.1813 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (heat capacity of water) and m = 40 g (mass of the 40 ml water).

steps.title: Report power and derived metrics
steps.instruction: Average the five power values (mean = 5.71 W). Compute power density (0.14 W cm⁻³) and intensity (0.41 W cm⁻²). Include the standard deviation (0.89 W, 0.02 W cm⁻³, 0.06 W cm⁻²) and relative standard deviation (16 %). Note that the higher power density in the beaker results from its smaller volume, while the intensity at the bath centre (transducer location) is larger than at the bottom of the beaker.
